source.title: Weeding Out Bad Seeds: Initial-Noise-Robust Unlearning for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
source.authors: Arian Komaei Koma; Seyed Amir Kasaei; Aida Aryafar; Matin Ghiasi; Ali Aghayari; A. Souri; Mohammad Mosayyebi; A. M. Sadeghzadeh; M. Rohban

page_placements.theme: Diffusion concept erasure undone by prompts, noise and fine-tuning

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether concept removal in text-to-image diffusion models survives changes to initial noise and prompt-based adversarial attacks, extending the unlearning-robustness question to a different modality from the LLM claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own results for random-noise re-emergence and for Ring-A-Bell and UnlearnDiffAtk attacks. Cited results from other papers are not recorded. Hyperparameter-selection and classifier-diagnostic values are omitted unless they measure an attack or re-emergence outcome.
record.test_reason: The versions concern LLM unlearning (targeted-knowledge accuracy, general ability), as do all three original sources. This study tests concept erasure (nudity, style, objects) in text-to-image diffusion models: SD 1.4, SD 2.1, SD3 and FLUX. That is a different kind of system, so no row measures what a version names. Its attack results under Ring-A-Bell and UnlearnDiffAtk are analogues of E and F in diffusion models, not tests of them, and are recorded under fits_no_version. It does not cite the LLM originals. It only discusses the broader idea that erasure may block access rather than remove.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors identify 'probabilistic forgetting': erased concepts re-emerge under other initial noise, in up to 55% of generations among fixed-seed-safe prompts across the evaluated methods. Adaptive Noise Sampling lowers re-emergence, failure counts and ASR, with competitive quality and better non-target retention. They state the results show reduced probabilistic forgetting, not certified worst-case removal.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces Adaptive Noise Sampling, which changes the initialization-noise sampling and weighting used during iterative diffusion-model unlearning. It is not a reproduction of an LLM unlearning method.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success and re-emergence vary by unlearning method; Adaptive Noise Sampling reduces but does not eliminate attack success for several methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Black-box Ring-A-Bell recovery prompts recover nudity from standard ESD (45.68% ASR) and EAP (53.13%). They barely work on ACE (0.20%) and RECELER (1.38%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-based attacks recover erased concepts from some unlearned text-to-image diffusion models, with strong dependence on the erasure method.

fits_no_version.finding: White-box UnlearnDiffAtk adversarial prompts recover nudity from standard ESD at 76.35% ASR, and from RECELER and EAP at about 19-22%. ACE shows 2.81%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimized adversarial prompts recover erased concepts from several diffusion unlearning methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Adaptive Noise Sampling lowers attack success against each paired baseline but does not eliminate it. Examples: ESD 45.68%→35.55% under Ring-A-Bell and 76.35%→23.28% under UnlearnDiffAtk; EAP 53.13%→32.38%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concentrating diffusion unlearning updates on concept-triggering initial noise reduces, but does not remove, prompt-attack recovery.

fits_no_version.finding: Among prompts that pass the fixed-seed test, nudity re-emerges under other random seeds in 4-25% of generations for the four baselines. With adaptive sampling this falls to 0.5-10%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diffusion concept erasure evaluated at a fixed seed overstates removal; varying only the initial noise re-exposes the concept.

record.problems: The evaluated systems are text-to-image diffusion models rather than LLMs. The attack-success table gives point estimates without uncertainty. The authors also state that finite sampling cannot certify worst-case concept removal.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported results, including style and object removal, classifier-corruption ablations, quality metrics, and additional architecture scaling, were left out because they do not directly measure the listed attack versions or the random-noise re-emergence finding captured here.

untested.parts: No LLM unlearning or knowledge-accuracy evaluation; diffusion concept erasure only.
No activation-direction ablation or internal-edit analysis.
No LLM prompting attacks. Ring-A-Bell and UnlearnDiffAtk prompt attacks are tested on diffusion models only.
Adaptive Noise Sampling is a diffusion-model method. It is not tested on LLMs or against fine-tuning, internal-edit or quantization attacks.

record.verdict_notes: This is a judgement call. One could treat diffusion models as a 'new setting' (T3) and link the Ring-A-Bell and UnlearnDiffAtk rows to E and F. I did not, because the versions and all originals concern LLM knowledge unlearning, and the row-linking rule requires the same kind of system. If the phenomenon is broadened to generative-model unlearning, R5/R7/R13 would support an E-analogue; R1/R3/R9 would show ACE and RECELER resisting it; and R2-R16 would limit the scope of an F-analogue, since attacks are reduced but not eliminated. No uncertainty is reported for Table 18. Ring-A-Bell ASRs are computed over 4,000 generations from the 20-seed evaluation.

versions.untested_parts: The study is on text-to-image diffusion models, not LLMs, and does not establish near-chance targeted-knowledge accuracy together with general ability under the version's conditions.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or small relearning set is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether a method blocks access rather than deletes knowledge is reported.
No weight quantization attack is tested.
Tests Ring-A-Bell prompt-based recovery attacks, but does not separately test rephrasing, other languages, or in-context information.
Tests the adaptive method against Ring-A-Bell and UnlearnDiffAtk, but not against fine-tuning, internal-edit, or quantization attacks.

relation.reason: The study discusses the broader phenomenon (apparent erasure that is not robust) in diffusion models. It cites none of the original sources, and LLMs appear only in one reference title.

tranche.reason: Concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models (SD 1.4, 2.1, 3, FLUX), not LLM unlearning. The versions concern LLM targeted knowledge, so this is a different kind of system. The study neither tests nor uses the versions.

source_check.notes: All four UDA ASR values are the Base (pre-Adaptive Noise Sampling) numbers on SD 1.4 nudity. The study also gives the with-method values: 2.42, 11.88, 23.28 and 15.58. No verdicts are given.

statements.problem: Numbers match Table 18 Base checkpoints under UDA: ESD 76.35, RECELER 19.14, EAP 21.74, ACE 2.81. Setting is SD 1.4 nudity erasure, not LLMs.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The reported attack success rate is 53.13%, indicating recovery in this tested condition (R7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ESD and adaptive checkpoints under Ring-A-Bell
reader_labels.reason: Recovery is incomplete and varies by checkpoint: ESD ASR is 45.68% and 35.55%, while adaptive EAP and RECELER retain nonzero ASRs (R4, R6, R8).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Recovery is low for the standard ACE and RECELER checkpoints and is absent for adaptive ACE (R1-R4).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Adaptive Noise Sampling checkpoints under Ring-A-Bell
reader_labels.reason: The adaptive checkpoints reduce ASR relative to their paired standard checkpoints, including reducing ACE ASR to 0.00% (R2, R4, R6, R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Adaptive ESD, EAP, and RECELER checkpoints under Ring-A-Bell
reader_labels.reason: The adaptive method lowers attack success but does not eliminate it for these checkpoints (R4, R6, R8).
